The '''geometric set cover problem''' is the special case of the [[set cover problem]] in geometric settings. The input is a range space <math>\Sigma = (X, \mathcal{R})</math> where <math>X</math> is a [[Universe (mathematics)|universe]] of points in <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math> and <math>\mathcal{R}</math> is a family of subsets of <math>X</math> called ''ranges'', defined by the [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of <math>X</math> and geometric shapes such as disks and axis-parallel rectangles. The goal is to select a ''minimum-size'' subset <math>\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{R}</math> of ranges such that every point in the universe <math>X</math> is covered by some range in <math>\mathcal{C}</math>.

Given the same range space <math>\Sigma</math>, a closely related problem is the '''geometric hitting set problem''', where the goal is to select a ''minimum-size'' subset <math>H \subseteq X</math> of points such that every range of <math>\mathcal{R}</math> has nonempty intersection with <math>H</math>, i.e., is ''hit'' by <math>H</math>.

In the one-dimensional case, where <math>X</math> contains points on the [[real line]] and <math>\mathcal{R}</math> is defined by intervals, both the geometric set cover and hitting set problems can be solved in [[Time complexity|polynomial time]] using a simple [[greedy algorithm]]. However, in higher dimensions, they are known to be [[NP-completeness|NP-complete]] even for simple shapes, i.e., when <math>\mathcal{R}</math> is induced by unit disks or unit squares.<ref name="npc">{{Citation
| last1 = Fowler | first1  = R.J. | last2 = Paterson | first2 = M.S. | last3 = Tanimoto | first3 = S.L.
| title = Optimal packing and covering in the plane are NP-complete
| journal = Inf. Process. Lett.
| volume  = 12 | issue  = 3 | pages  = 133–137 | year    = 1981
| doi  = 10.1016/0020-0190(81)90111-3 }}</ref> The '''discrete unit disc cover problem''' is a geometric version of the general set cover problem which is [[NP-hardness|NP-hard]].<ref>https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~alopez-o/files/OtDUDCP_2011.pdf On the Discrete Unit Disk Cover Problem</ref>

Many [[approximation algorithm]]s have been devised for these problems. Due to the geometric nature, the approximation ratios for these problems can be much better than the general set cover/hitting set problems. Moreover, these approximate solutions can even be computed in near-linear time.<ref name="AP14">
{{cite conference
 | first1 = Pankaj K.
 | last1 = Agarwal
 | first2 = Jiangwei
 | last2 = Pan
 | title = Near-Linear Algorithms for Geometric Hitting Sets and Set Covers
 | book-title = Proceedings of the thirtieth annual symposium on Computational Geometry
 | year = 2014 }}</ref>

==Approximation algorithms==

The [[set cover problem#greedy algorithm|greedy algorithm]] for the general set cover problem gives <math>O(\log n)</math> approximation, where <math>n = \max\{|X|, |\mathcal{R}|\}</math>.  This approximation is known to be tight up to constant factor.<ref name="lower_bound">{{Citation
| last = Feige | first  = Uriel
| title = A threshold of ln n for approximating set cover
| journal = Journal of the ACM
| year    = 1998
| doi     = 10.1145/285055.285059
 | volume=45
 | issue  = 4
| pages=634–652
| citeseerx  = 10.1.1.70.5014
| s2cid = 52827488
}}</ref> However, in geometric settings, better approximations can be obtained.  Using a [[Multiplicative Weight Update Method|multiplicative weight algorithm]],<ref>{{Citation
| last1 = Arora
| first1 = S. 
| last2 = Hazan 
| first2 = E.
| last3 = Kale
| first3 = S.
| title = The Multiplicative Weights Update Method: a Meta-Algorithm and Applications
| journal = Theory of Computing
| volume = 8 
| pages = 121–164 
| year    = 2012
| doi = 10.4086/toc.2012.v008a006 
| doi-access = free
}}</ref> Brönnimann and Goodrich<ref name="BG95">{{Citation
| last1 = Brönnimann | first1 = H. | last2 = Goodrich | first2 = M.
| title = Almost optimal set covers in finite VC-dimension
| journal = Discrete & Computational Geometry
| year    = 1995
| doi = 10.1007/bf02570718
 | volume=14
 | issue = 4 | pages=463–479
| doi-access = free}}</ref> showed that an <math>O(\log \mathsf{OPT})</math>-approximate set cover/hitting set for a range space <math>\Sigma</math> with constant VC-dimension can be computed in polynomial time, where <math>\mathsf{OPT} \le n</math> denotes the size of the optimal solution. The approximation ratio can be further improved to <math>O(\log \log \mathsf{OPT})</math> or <math>O(1)</math> when <math>\mathcal{R}</math> is induced by axis-parallel rectangles or disks in <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>, respectively.

==Near-linear-time algorithms==

Based on the iterative-reweighting technique of Clarkson<ref>{{Cite book|publisher = [[Springer Berlin Heidelberg]]|date = 1993-08-11|isbn = 978-3-540-57155-1|pages = 246–252|series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science|doi = 10.1007/3-540-57155-8_252|first = Kenneth L.|last = Clarkson|editor-first = Frank|editor-last = Dehne|editor-first2 = Jörg-Rüdiger|editor-last2 = Sack|editor-first3 = Nicola|editor-last3 = Santoro|editor-first4 = Sue|display-editors = 3 |editor-last4 = Whitesides|title = Algorithms and Data Structures|volume = 709|chapter = Algorithms for polytope covering and approximation}}</ref> and Brönnimann and Goodrich,<ref name="BG95" /> Agarwal and Pan<ref name="AP14" /> gave algorithms that computes an approximate set cover/hitting set of a geometric range space in <math>O(n~\mathrm{polylog}(n))</math> time. For example, their algorithms computes an <math>O(\log \log \mathsf{OPT})</math>-approximate hitting set in <math>O(n \log^3n\log\log\log \mathsf{OPT})</math> time for range spaces induced by 2D axis-parallel rectangles; and it computes an <math>O(1)</math>-approximate set cover in <math>O(n \log^4n)</math> time for range spaces induced by 2D disks.
